questions.enonce_markdown:
As the first king in Israel, Saul failed to live up to God’s expectations.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The printed question gives a statement without an instruction verb, so it is answered as a "discuss" question: to what extent did Saul, the first king of Israel, fail to meet what God expected of him? The sources are 1 Samuel 9-31. The evidence supports the claim, although Saul also had real achievements.

**1. Evidence that he failed.**
(i) *Unauthorised sacrifice at Gilgal (1 Samuel 13).* Facing the Philistines, Saul grew impatient, did not wait for Samuel and offered the burnt offering himself. Samuel told him that his kingdom would not continue.
(ii) *Disobedience in the war against Amalek (1 Samuel 15).* He was ordered to put Amalek under the ban, but he spared King Agag and kept the best of the animals, claiming they were for sacrifice. Samuel replied, "to obey is better than sacrifice", and announced that God had rejected him as king.
(iii) *The rash oath (1 Samuel 14).* He forbade the army to eat during the battle; the people were weakened, and Jonathan, who did not know of the oath, was almost put to death.
(iv) *Jealousy and persecution of David (1 Samuel 18-26).* When David won popularity, Saul repeatedly tried to kill him, and the king's attention was diverted from the defence of the nation.
(v) *The killing of the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22).* This was an act of cruelty against the priestly family that had helped David.
(vi) *Consulting the medium of Endor (1 Samuel 28).* Cut off from God's guidance, he turned to a practice forbidden by the law, and he died on Mount Gilboa with his sons (1 Samuel 31).

**2. Evidence that points the other way.** Saul began well: he was chosen by God, was humble at the start (he hid among the baggage, 10:22), and received the Spirit of God. He delivered Jabesh-gilead (ch. 11), fought the Philistines and other enemies, and unified the tribes in a first national army. His failures were not about lack of ability but about trust and obedience.

**3. Why the standard was high.** The king was expected to be God's servant, to rule under the covenant and to obey the word delivered by the prophet (compare Samuel's speech in 1 Samuel 12). Saul tried to place his own judgement above God's word.

**Conclusion.** The statement is largely justified: Saul was rejected because of repeated disobedience, impatience, jealousy and lack of trust in God, even though he had military successes. His reign served as a warning and prepared the way for David.
